name: ProtoSnap: Prototype Alignment for Cuneiform Signs
date: arXiv preprint 2502.00129 submitted 31 January 2025; Cornell Chronicle press release 4 March 2025; presented at ICLR 2025 (International Conference on Learning Representations, Singapore, April 2025)
creator: Rachel Mikulinsky and Morris Alper (co-first authors, Tel Aviv University), Shai Gordin (Ariel University), Enrique Jiménez (LMU Munich, head of the Electronic Babylonian Library), Yoram Cohen (Tel Aviv University, archaeology) and Hadar Averbuch-Elor (Cornell Tech / Cornell Bowers CIS, formerly TAU). Code released by TAU-VAILab on GitHub
form: Machine-learning method and model: an unsupervised alignment technique using features from a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion model, plus a ControlNet generator for synthetic sign images and a new expert-annotated benchmark (272 images). Code, data and trained models released
effect_on_arc: None directly. ProtoSnap has not recovered any Gilgamesh text, and the paper does not mention the epic. Its effect is upstream: better sign recognition on photographed tablets could speed the reading of unpublished fragments, some of which may belong to the epic, as the eBL Fragmentarium (whose data it uses) has already shown for Gilgamesh
critical_response: Accepted as a conference paper at ICLR 2025, a top-tier machine-learning venue. Covered by the Cornell Chronicle, Cornell Tech, Phys.org and popular tech outlets (March 2025). The paper reports ProtoSnap beats generic feature-matching baselines (SIFT, DINOv2, DIFT) at aligning prototypes to real signs. No substantial published Assyriological critique found [uncertain]
controversies: No notable controversy. The authors state their own limits: the method 'will still fail if the scan displays a structurally different variant' of a sign, and struggles with extreme deformation or low-quality tablets. Wider debate about AI in Assyriology (hype versus the scarce pool of human experts) applies but is not specific to this paper
regional_reception: No Iraqi or Kurdish reception identified [uncertain]. The work is an Israeli, German and US collaboration; the training images come from the eBL collection of photographs, largely of British Museum tablets excavated in Iraq
method: Sign recognition via prototype alignment. Given a photo of a single cuneiform sign and a 'prototype' (a clean font rendering with an annotated stroke skeleton, from the Santakku and SantakkuM fonts by Sylvie Vanséveren), a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion model supplies per-pixel features. The system builds a 4D similarity volume, finds 'best-buddy' mutual nearest-neighbour matches, fits a global affine transform, then refines each stroke separately by optimisation so the template 'snaps' onto the wedges actually impressed in the clay. The aligned skeletons then condition a ControlNet that generates realistic, structurally correct synthetic sign images to train a sign classifier
ai_pipeline_stage: Sign recognition (the reading step): locating the structure of individual signs in tablet photographs and generating synthetic training data for OCR. It does not do imaging, fragment joining or translation
scale_metrics: Diffusion model fine-tuned on 34,868 sign images covering 362 sign types from the eBL dataset (about 40% Neo-Babylonian, about 20% Neo-Assyrian, plus Ur III, Old Babylonian, Middle Babylonian and other periods; Akkadian and Sumerian). Test benchmark: 272 expert-annotated images of 25 sign types with 2 to 8 strokes each. Adding ControlNet synthetic data lifted classifier accuracy from 58.43% to 64.14%, balanced accuracy from 34.57% to 43.57%, and accuracy on rare signs (under 50 examples) from 25.84% to 53.17%. Context: an estimated 500,000 cuneiform tablets in museums and over 1,000 distinct signs
what_was_found: No text was found. The output is a tool: a way to map the stroke structure of a sign on a real tablet photo, a released benchmark, and a generator of synthetic training images that roughly doubles recognition accuracy for rare signs
provenance_and_ethics: Legitimate academic data: sign images from the Electronic Babylonian Library (LMU Munich) cuneiform OCR dataset, drawing on British Museum photographs of tablets largely excavated in Iraq in the 19th century. Code, data and models released openly on GitHub (TAU-VAILab/ProtoSnap). No repatriation issue specific to the project; the physical tablets remain in the British Museum and other Western collections [uncertain: exact licence terms of the image data]
ai_craft_tension: ProtoSnap is a clear case of the machine sitting at the reading step and still needing humans on both sides of it. Before: the prototypes are human-made fonts and the 272 benchmark signs were annotated by expert paleographers. After: the model only says 'this is where the strokes of sign X are'; deciding which sign a damaged wedge cluster is, what word it spells and how the line reads is still the Assyriologist's job. The authors admit it fails when a scribe used a structurally different variant, which is exactly where human paleographic judgement matters most. Its real contribution is scarcity relief: in Averbuch-Elor's words, there are endless 2D scans but very little labelled data, and synthetic signs let a small expert labour pool go further. For Gilgamesh, that means faster first-pass reading of the unpublished fragments where missing lines might hide, not a machine that reads the epic
essay_hooks: (1) Averbuch-Elor: 'There's an endless amount of 2D scans of these cuneiforms, but the amount of labeled data is very scarce' (Cornell Chronicle, 4 March 2025). (2) Yoram Cohen: the aim is 'to increase the ancient sources available to us by tenfold' (Cornell Chronicle). (3) Rare-sign accuracy jumped from 25.84% to 53.17% with synthetic training data (ICLR 2025 paper). (4) An image model built to make pictures (Stable Diffusion) repurposed to read 3,000-year-old wedges. (5) The template comes from a modern font (Santakku), so the machine learns the ancient hand by comparing it to a typeface. (6) Its own admitted failure case, a scribe's variant form of a sign, is the thing a trained human reader handles best. (7) About 500,000 tablets in museums, only a fraction published (Cornell Chronicle). Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00129 ; https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2025/03/ai-models-make-precise-copies-cuneiform-characters ; https://tau-vailab.github.io/ProtoSnap/
